title: Fragility Index: A New Approach for Binary Classification

problem.claim: Binary classification applications need metrics that capture not only whether error exceeds a threshold but also the magnitude of that error.

gap.claim: Existing performance metrics focus on the probability of threshold-exceeding error and generally fail to capture how large the error is beyond the threshold.

contributions.claim: The paper proposes the Fragility Index to evaluate binary classifiers by capturing the magnitude of error.
The paper combines distributionally robust optimization and robust satisficing to control the maximum degree of classifier fragility under sample-distribution shifts.
The paper shows that the Fragility Index can be calculated and optimized for common probabilistic distance measures.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors explicitly describe the Fragility Index as a novel metric.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that experiments with real datasets demonstrate new insights from the Fragility Index.
The authors report that classifiers selected under the Fragility Index improve robustness and reduce the risk of large errors relative to classifiers selected by alternative metrics.

narrative_sequence.summary: Binary classification metrics commonly assess whether error exceeds a threshold.
These metrics emphasize probability and overlook the magnitude of threshold-exceeding error, which matters in applications such as disease detection and credit-default prediction.
The authors introduce the Fragility Index and pair it with robust optimization approaches to penalize large errors and manage fragility under distribution shifts.
The Fragility Index is reported to be calculable and optimizable for common probabilistic distance measures.
Experiments on real datasets are reported to show new insights and improved robustness with lower risk of large errors compared with alternative metrics.

unknowns: The abstract does not define the mathematical form of the Fragility Index.
The abstract does not specify the datasets, baselines, experimental settings, or quantitative results.
The abstract does not detail the probabilistic distance measures or optimization procedure.
